opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that it's an ambitious goal, and we chose it deliberately. We're not saying we're confident we'll succeed in four years. But having a concrete deadline forces you to prioritize and ask: what would we actually need to have done by then for this to work?

The key thing is that the goal isn't to solve every alignment problem ourselves, by hand, for superintelligent systems. That would be really hard, and I don't think it's realistic on that timeline. The goal is more like building a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher. If we can build a system that's about as good as we are at alignment research, and we can trust that it's actually aligned and doing what we want, then we can use lots of copies of it to make much faster progress on the harder problems: aligning the next generation of systems, and eventually superintelligence.

So that breaks the problem into more tractable pieces. First, can we develop scalable training methods, things like using AI to help humans evaluate tasks that are too hard for them to evaluate alone? Second, can we validate that the system we've built is actually aligned? That's where interpretability, and studying whether models generalize the way we want, come in. Third, can we stress test the whole pipeline? For example, can we deliberately train misaligned models and check that our techniques catch them?

Why four years? Partly because nobody really knows how fast capabilities will progress, and it seems plausible that we could have very powerful systems within this decade. I'd rather we be early than late. If it turns out we have more time, great. But I really don't want to be in a world where these systems arrive and we haven't done the work.

I also think it's important to be honest that this might not work. If, after a couple of years, our techniques aren't panning out, then we should say so loudly. That's useful information too, both for the lab and for the world, because then you need to slow down or take a different approach. But I'm actually fairly optimistic. A lot of things have gone better than I expected. Language models understand a lot about human values and what we want, and that gives us a lot to work with. The question is whether we can make that work reliably as systems get much more capable than us.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would rather be early than late and worries about systems arriving before the work is done, but it does not clearly state that the aim is to solve superintelligence alignment well before it becomes necessary.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls the goal ambitious and deliberately sets a four-year deadline, while explaining that the work should be broken into more tractable pieces and that success is uncertain. This communicates balancing ambition with perceived achievability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the four-year goal is deliberately ambitious. The way I think about it is: we're not trying to solve the full problem of aligning a superintelligence directly, because honestly, I don't think humans are going to be able to do that by hand. The systems we're worried about will be smarter than us, and evaluating what they're doing is going to be really hard for us to do unaided.

So the goal is actually a bit more specific than "solve alignment in four years." It's to build a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher. If we can get an AI system that's about as good as a strong alignment researcher, and we can trust it, then we can run lots of copies of it, have it work on the problem, and essentially bootstrap our way to aligning much more capable systems. That's the core bet: the first system we need to align well enough doesn't have to be superintelligent, it just has to be good enough to do alignment research.

And the four years is partly about urgency. I think there's a real chance we get very capable systems this decade, and I'd rather we have a plan that's grounded in a concrete deadline than one that says "we'll figure it out eventually." Setting a timeline forces you to prioritize. It forces you to ask, what are the actual bottlenecks? Things like scalable oversight, interpretability, understanding generalization, deliberately training misaligned models to stress-test our pipeline.

Do I think we'll definitely succeed? No. I'd say I'm optimistic, but it's a bet. The failure mode I worry about more is that we don't try hard enough, or we don't try in a focused way. So part of the point of announcing the goal publicly is to commit to it, to put real compute and real people behind it, and to be honest if it's not working. If in two years it looks like this approach is failing, that's really important information, and we should say so loudly and change course.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as an ambitious research goal, rather than a prediction that we’ll definitely have solved alignment in four years. The point is to work backwards from the problem we ultimately need to solve: how do we reliably steer and control systems that are much smarter than we are?

One approach is to use AI to help us do alignment research. If we can align a system that’s capable enough to substantially accelerate that work, we can use it to help figure out how to align the next, more capable system. But that puts a lot of weight on our ability to evaluate the research it produces. We can’t just ask a model whether it’s aligned and take its word for it.

So I’d want success to mean having a concrete approach, and strong evidence that it works—even when the system can understand things that its human supervisors can’t. Four years gives us a deadline to organise around. It doesn’t mean the underlying scientific uncertainty goes away.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a very ambitious research goal, rather than a prediction that we’ll have solved the whole problem in four years. We don’t know how far away superintelligence is, and we don’t know how hard alignment will turn out to be. But we need to make progress before those systems arrive, so it’s useful to set a deadline that forces us to work backwards from what we would actually need.

And “solving alignment” needs some unpacking. We want to be able to reliably steer and control a system that is much smarter than we are. We can’t just look at its answers and say, “That seems good,” because it might be doing things we don’t understand, or finding problems that we couldn’t have found ourselves.

The central idea is to use AI to help us do the alignment research. If we can align a system that’s capable enough to be a really useful research assistant, then we can use it to help us align the next, more capable system. But that doesn’t remove the hard part: we still need evidence that our methods work, including in situations where humans can’t directly evaluate the work. So I’d judge the goal by whether we have a convincing technical case for that, rather than just whether we’ve reached a date on the calendar.

r001.rationale: It says progress is needed before superintelligent systems arrive, but does not state that the aim is to solve alignment well before then.

r002.rationale: It calls the goal ambitious and explains the deadline’s usefulness, but does not say the four-year deadline was chosen to balance ambition with perceived achievability.
